\section{Overview}

Declarations of the Lean module \texttt{FABL.Chapter02.NoiseStability.NoiseKernels}.

\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Independent product probability mass function]
\lean{FABL.independentProductPMF}
\label{FABL.independentProductPMF}
\leanok
Let $\iota$ be a finite index type, let $\alpha_i$ be a finite type for each
$i\in\iota$, and let $p_i$ be a probability mass function on $\alpha_i$. The independent
product probability mass function on tuples $x=(x_i)_{i\in\iota}$ assigns mass
$\prod_{i\in\iota}p_i(x_i)$ to $x$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Point probabilities of an independent product]
\lean{FABL.independentProductPMF_apply}
\label{FABL.independentProductPMF_apply}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.independentProductPMF}
\difficulty{1}
Let $I$ be a finite index set, let $A_i$ be a finite set for each $i\in I$, and choose a
probability mass function $p_i$ on each $A_i$. The independent product distribution on
tuples $x=(x_i)_{i\in I}$ assigns probability $\prod_{i\in I}p_i(x_i)$ to $x$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Correlation keep probability]
\lean{FABL.correlationKeepProbability}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p053-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p120-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p214-b005
}
\label{FABL.correlationKeepProbability}
\leanok
For $\rho\in[-1,1]$, the correlation keep probability is the nonnegative real number
$(1+\rho)/2$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Upper bound for the keep probability]
\lean{FABL.correlationKeepProbability_le_one}
\label{FABL.correlationKeepProbability_le_one}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.correlationKeepProbability}
\difficulty{3}
For every real number $\rho\in[-1,1]$, the probability $(1+\rho)/2$ is at most $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Coordinate sign noise]
\lean{FABL.coordinateNoisePMF}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p053-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p120-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p214-b005,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p260-b001,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p260-b002
}
\statementsource{mossel-neeman-gaussian-noise-stability}{pdf-b53c1a5aa27d-p007-b003}
\label{FABL.coordinateNoisePMF}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.correlationKeepProbability, FABL.correlationKeepProbability_le_one}
Let $\rho\in[-1,1]$ and let $x\in\{\pm1\}$. Define a random sign by keeping $x$ with the
correlation keep probability associated with $\rho$, and otherwise replacing it by $-x$;
the resulting probability mass function is the coordinate noise distribution at $x$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Nonnegative correlation probability]
\lean{FABL.nonnegativeCorrelationProbability}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p053-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p120-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p214-b005
}
\label{FABL.nonnegativeCorrelationProbability}
\leanok
For $\rho\in[0,1]$, define the nonnegative correlation probability to be the real number
$\rho$, regarded as a nonnegative real.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Upper bound for nonnegative correlation probability]
\lean{FABL.nonnegativeCorrelationProbability_le_one}
\label{FABL.nonnegativeCorrelationProbability_le_one}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.nonnegativeCorrelationProbability}
\difficulty{1}
For every $\rho\in[0,1]$, the nonnegative correlation probability associated with $\rho$
is at most $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Coordinate resampling noise]
\lean{FABL.coordinateResamplingNoisePMF}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p053-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p120-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p214-b005
}
\statementsource{mossel-neeman-gaussian-noise-stability}{pdf-b53c1a5aa27d-p007-b003}
\label{FABL.coordinateResamplingNoisePMF}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.nonnegativeCorrelationProbability, FABL.nonnegativeCorrelationProbability_le_one, FABL.uniformPMF}
Let $\rho\in[0,1]$ and let $x\in\{\pm1\}$. Define a random sign by retaining $x$ with
probability $\rho$ and, with probability $1-\rho$, drawing a sign uniformly from
$\{\pm1\}$; the resulting probability mass function is the coordinate resampling noise
distribution at $x$.
\end{definition}

Let $\rho\in[0,1]$ and let $x$ be a sign. The distribution obtained by retaining $x$
with probability $\rho$ and otherwise drawing a uniformly random sign is equal to the
distribution obtained by retaining $x$ with probability $(1+\rho)/2$ and replacing it by
its negative otherwise.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Independent coordinate noise kernel]
\lean{FABL.noiseKernel}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p055-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p120-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p124-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p214-b005,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p214-b006
}
\statementsource{mossel-neeman-gaussian-noise-stability}{
  pdf-b53c1a5aa27d-p007-b003,
  pdf-b53c1a5aa27d-p034-b004
}
\label{FABL.noiseKernel}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.coordinateNoisePMF, FABL.independentProductPMF}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $\rho\in[-1,1]$, and let $x\in\{\pm1\}^n$. Define a
probability distribution on $\{\pm1\}^n$ by independently applying the coordinate sign
noise distribution, with parameter $\rho$, to each coordinate of $x$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Independent coordinate resampling kernel]
\lean{FABL.resamplingNoiseKernel}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p053-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p120-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p214-b005,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p214-b006
}
\statementsource{mossel-neeman-gaussian-noise-stability}{pdf-b53c1a5aa27d-p007-b003}
\label{FABL.resamplingNoiseKernel}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.coordinateResamplingNoisePMF, FABL.independentProductPMF}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $\rho\in[0,1]$, and let $x\in\{\pm1\}^n$. Define a
probability distribution on $\{\pm1\}^n$ by independently retaining each coordinate of
$x$ with probability $\rho$ and otherwise replacing it by an independent uniform sign.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Correlated sign-vector pair distribution]
\lean{FABL.correlatedPairPMF}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p053-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p120-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p214-b005,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p260-b001,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p260-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p260-b005
}
\statementsource{mossel-neeman-gaussian-noise-stability}{pdf-b53c1a5aa27d-p007-b003}
\label{FABL.correlatedPairPMF}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.noiseKernel, FABL.uniformPMF}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $\rho\in[-1,1]$. Choose $X$ uniformly from
$\{\pm1\}^n$, then draw $Y$ from the independent coordinate noise kernel with parameter
$\rho$ applied to $X$. The resulting joint probability distribution is that of $(X,Y)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Correlated sign pair distribution]
\lean{FABL.correlatedSignPairPMF}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p053-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p120-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p214-b005,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p260-b001,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p260-b002
}
\statementsource{mossel-neeman-gaussian-noise-stability}{pdf-b53c1a5aa27d-p007-b003}
\label{FABL.correlatedSignPairPMF}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.coordinateNoisePMF, FABL.uniformPMF}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $\rho\in[-1,1]$. Choose $X$ uniformly from
$\{\pm1\}$, then draw $Y$ from the coordinate sign noise distribution with parameter
$\rho$ applied to $X$. The resulting joint probability distribution is that of $(X,Y)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Point probabilities of the correlated sign law]
\lean{FABL.correlatedSignPairPMF_apply}
\label{FABL.correlatedSignPairPMF_apply}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.coordinateNoisePMF, FABL.correlatedSignPairPMF, FABL.uniformPMF}
\difficulty{4}
Let $\rho\in[-1,1]$, and let $X,Y$ be signs. The probability of the pair $(X,Y)$ under
the correlated sign law is the product of the uniform probability of $X$ and the
conditional noise probability of obtaining $Y$ from $X$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Symmetry of coordinate noise probabilities]
\lean{FABL.coordinateNoisePMF_apply_comm}
\label{FABL.coordinateNoisePMF_apply_comm}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.coordinateNoisePMF, FABL.correlationKeepProbability, FABL.correlationKeepProbability_le_one}
\difficulty{4}
Let $\rho\in[-1,1]$, and let $x,y\in\{−1,1\}$. Under the coordinate noise rule that
keeps its input sign with probability $(1+\rho)/2$ and flips it otherwise, the
probability of moving from $x$ to $y$ equals the probability of moving from $y$ to $x$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Symmetry of the noise kernel]
\lean{FABL.noiseKernel_apply_comm}
\label{FABL.noiseKernel_apply_comm}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.coordinateNoisePMF_apply_comm, FABL.independentProductPMF_apply, FABL.noiseKernel}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $\rho\in[-1,1]$, and let $x,y\in\{-1,1\}^n$. The noise
kernel with parameter $\rho$, evaluated at $x$ and $y$, has the same value when the two
vectors are interchanged.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Point probabilities of a correlated pair]
\lean{FABL.correlatedPairPMF_apply}
\label{FABL.correlatedPairPMF_apply}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.correlatedPairPMF, FABL.noiseKernel, FABL.uniformPMF}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $\rho\in[-1,1]$, and let $x,y\in\{\pm1\}^n$. For a random pair
$(X,Y)$ formed by choosing $X$ uniformly from the cube and applying independent
coordinate noise to obtain $Y$, with each coordinate retained with probability
$(1+\rho)/2$, its point probability is $\mathbb P((X,Y)=(x,y))=2^{-n}\,\mathbb P(Y=y\mid
X=x)$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{4}
Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $\rho\in[-1,1]$, and let $(X,Y)$ be the correlated pair of sign
vectors on $\{\pm1\}^n$ obtained by choosing $X$ uniformly and applying independent
coordinate noise with retention probability $(1+\rho)/2$. The law of $(Y,X)$ equals the
law of $(X,Y)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[One-coordinate sign cube equivalence]
\lean{FABL.signCubeOneEquiv}
\label{FABL.signCubeOneEquiv}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign}
The set of functions from a singleton to $\{−1,1\}$ is equivalent to the group of units
of the integers, whose elements are $−1$ and $1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[One-coordinate sign pair equivalence]
\lean{FABL.signPairCubeOneEquiv}
\label{FABL.signPairCubeOneEquiv}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.signCubeOneEquiv}
The product of two sets of functions from a singleton to $\{−1,1\}$ is equivalent to the
product of two copies of the group of units of the integers; the equivalence applies the
one-coordinate sign equivalence to each component.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[One-coordinate correlated pair law]
\lean{FABL.correlatedPairPMF_one_map_signPairCubeOneEquiv}
\label{FABL.correlatedPairPMF_one_map_signPairCubeOneEquiv}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.correlatedPairPMF, FABL.correlatedPairPMF_apply, FABL.correlatedSignPairPMF, FABL.correlatedSignPairPMF_apply, FABL.noiseKernel, FABL.signCubeOneEquiv, FABL.signPairCubeOneEquiv, FABL.uniformPMF}
\difficulty{4}
For every correlation parameter $\rho\in[-1,1]$, the law of the pair of one-coordinate
cube points, transported to pairs of signs by the natural coordinate identification,
equals the law obtained by choosing the first sign uniformly and then retaining it with
probability $(1+\rho)/2$ or flipping it otherwise.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Expectation under a finite probability mass function]
\lean{FABL.pmfExpectation}
\label{FABL.pmfExpectation}
\leanok
Let $\Omega$ be a finite set, let $p$ be a probability mass function on $\Omega$, and
let $f\colon\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$. The expectation of $f$ under $p$ is
$\sum_{x\in\Omega}p(x)f(x)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Expectation as an integral]
\lean{FABL.pmfExpectation_eq_integral}
\label{FABL.pmfExpectation_eq_integral}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.pmfExpectation}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite measurable space in which every singleton is measurable, let
$p$ be a probability mass function on $\Omega$, and let $f:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$. The
expectation of $f$ under $p$ equals its integral with respect to the measure induced by
$p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Expectation under a mapped distribution]
\lean{FABL.pmfExpectation_map}
\label{FABL.pmfExpectation_map}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.pmfExpectation_eq_integral}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\Omega$ and $\Lambda$ be finite sets, let $p$ be a probability mass function on
$\Omega$, let $g:\Omega\to\Lambda$, and let $f:\Lambda\to\mathbb{R}$. The expectation of
$f$ under the distribution obtained by mapping $p$ through $g$ equals the expectation
under $p$ of the composite function $f\circ g$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Expectation of one]
\lean{FABL.pmfExpectation_const_one}
\label{FABL.pmfExpectation_const_one}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.pmfExpectation_eq_integral}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite set and let $p$ be a probability mass function on $\Omega$. The
expectation of the constant function with value $1$ is $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Expectation of a point mass]
\lean{FABL.pmfExpectation_pure}
\label{FABL.pmfExpectation_pure}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.pmfExpectation}
\difficulty{4}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite set, let $x\in\Omega$, and let $f:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$. The
expectation of $f$ under the probability mass function concentrated at $x$ is $f(x)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Expectation under a mixture]
\lean{FABL.pmfExpectation_bind}
\label{FABL.pmfExpectation_bind}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.pmfExpectation}
\difficulty{4}
Let $\Omega$ and $\Lambda$ be finite sets, let $P$ be a probability distribution on
$\Omega$, and for each $x\in\Omega$ let $Q_x$ be a probability distribution on
$\Lambda$. For any function $f:\Lambda\to\mathbb{R}$, its expectation under the
distribution obtained by first sampling from $P$ and then from $Q_x$ is the expectation
under $P$ of the conditional expectation under $Q_x$; that is, $\mathbb{E}_{x\sim
P,\,y\sim Q_x}[f(y)]=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim P}[\mathbb{E}_{y\sim Q_x}[f(y)]]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Scaling an expectation]
\lean{FABL.pmfExpectation_const_mul}
\label{FABL.pmfExpectation_const_mul}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.pmfExpectation}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite set, let $p$ be a probability mass function on $\Omega$, let
$c\in\bbr$, and let $f:\Omega\to\bbr$. The expectation of $x\mapsto c f(x)$ equals $c$
times the expectation of $f$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Scaling a probability expectation]
\lean{FABL.pmfExpectation_mul_const}
\label{FABL.pmfExpectation_mul_const}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.pmfExpectation}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite set, let $p$ be a probability mass function on $\Omega$, let
$f:\Omega\to\bbr$, and let $c\mathbin\bbr$. The expectation of the function $xmapsto f(x)c$
under $p$ equals $c$ times the expectation of $f$ under $p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Additivity of expectation]
\lean{FABL.pmfExpectation_add}
\label{FABL.pmfExpectation_add}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.pmfExpectation}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite set, let $p$ be a probability mass function on $\Omega$, and
let $f,g:\Omega\to\mathbb R$. Then $\mathbb E_p(f+g)=\mathbb E_p f+\mathbb E_p g$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Expectation of a finite sum]
\lean{FABL.pmfExpectation_sum}
\label{FABL.pmfExpectation_sum}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.pmfExpectation}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\Omega$ and $I$ be finite sets, let $p$ be a probability mass function on $\Omega$,
and let $f_i:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ for each $i\in I$. Then the expectation of the
pointwise sum is the sum of the expectations: $\mathbb{E}_p[\sum_{i\in I}f_i]=\sum_{i\in
I}\mathbb{E}_p[f_i]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Interchanging finite expectations]
\lean{FABL.fintypeExpectation_pmfExpectation_comm}
\label{FABL.fintypeExpectation_pmfExpectation_comm}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.pmfExpectation}
\difficulty{3}
Let $I$ be a finite nonempty set and let $a9$ be a finite set. For a probability mass
function $p$ on $a9$ and a function $f:I\timesa9\to\mathbb R$, the uniform average
over $i\in I$ of the expectation of $f(i,\cdot)$ under $p$ equals the expectation under
$p$ of the uniform average over $i\in I$ of $f(i,\cdot)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Expectation of a constant]
\lean{FABL.pmfExpectation_const}
\label{FABL.pmfExpectation_const}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.pmfExpectation_const_mul, FABL.pmfExpectation_const_one}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite set, let $p$ be a probability mass function on $\Omega$, and
let $c\in\bbr$. The expectation of the constant function with value $c$ is $c$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Monotonicity of probability expectation]
\lean{FABL.pmfExpectation_mono}
\label{FABL.pmfExpectation_mono}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.pmfExpectation}
\difficulty{1}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite set, let $p$ be a probability mass function on $\Omega$, and
let $f,g:\Omega\to\bbr$ satisfy $f(x)\langle g(x)$ for every $x$. Then the expectation of $f$
under $p$ is at most the expectation of $g$ under $p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Nonnegativity of finite expectation]
\lean{FABL.pmfExpectation_nonneg}
\label{FABL.pmfExpectation_nonneg}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.pmfExpectation_const, FABL.pmfExpectation_mono}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite set, let $p$ be a probability mass function on $\Omega$, and
let $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ satisfy $f(x)\ge 0$ for every $x\in\Omega$. Then
$\sum_{x\in\Omega}p(x)f(x)\ge 0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform expectation equals finite average]
\lean{FABL.pmfExpectation_uniformPMF_eq_expect}
\label{FABL.pmfExpectation_uniformPMF_eq_expect}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.integral_uniformPMF_eq_expect, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.pmfExpectation_eq_integral, FABL.uniformPMF}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty set and let $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R$. The expectation of
$f$ under the uniform probability distribution on $\Omega$ equals its uniform average,
$\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\sum_{x\in\Omega}f(x)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Pmf expectation coordinate noise pmf sign value]
\lean{FABL.pmfExpectation_coordinateNoisePMF_signValue}

\begin{theorem}[Expectation of a product under an independent law]
\lean{FABL.pmfExpectation_independentProductPMF_prod}
\label{FABL.pmfExpectation_independentProductPMF_prod}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.independentProductPMF, FABL.independentProductPMF_apply, FABL.pmfExpectation}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\iota$ be a finite set with decidable equality, let $\alpha_i$ be a finite set for
each $i\in\iota$, and let $p_i$ be a probability mass function on $\alpha_i$ and
$q_i:\alpha_i\to\mathbb{R}$. Under the independent product distribution, the expectation
of the product of the coordinate functions equals the product of their expectations:
$\mathbb{E}\bigl[\prod_{i\in\iota}q_i(X_i)\bigr]=\prod_{i\in\iota}\mathbb{E}_{p_i}[q_i]$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{5}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $\rho\in[-1,1]$, and let $x\in\{-1,1\}^n$. For every
subset $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$, the expectation of the $S$-monomial after
independently retaining each coordinate of $x$ with probability $(1+\rho)/2$ and
otherwise flipping its sign is $\rho^{|S|}$ times the $S$-monomial of $x$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Mean of a first-coordinate sign]
\lean{FABL.correlatedPairPMF_expect_signValue_fst}
\label{FABL.correlatedPairPMF_expect_signValue_fst}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.correlatedPairPMF, FABL.expect_monomial, FABL.monomial, FABL.noiseKernel, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.pmfExpectation_bind, FABL.pmfExpectation_const, FABL.pmfExpectation_map, FABL.pmfExpectation_uniformPMF_eq_expect, FABL.signValue}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $\rho\in[-1,1]$, and let $(X,Y)$ be the correlated pair of sign
vectors on $\{\pm1\}^n$ obtained by choosing $X$ uniformly and applying independent
coordinate noise with retention probability $(1+\rho)/2$. For every coordinate
$i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, the expected value of $X_i$ is zero.
\end{theorem}

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $\rho\in[-1,1]$, and let $(X,Y)$ be the correlated pair of sign
vectors on $\{\pm1\}^n$ obtained by choosing $X$ uniformly and applying independent
coordinate noise with retention probability $(1+\rho)/2$. For every coordinate
$i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, the expected product $X_iY_i$ equals $\rho$.
\end{theorem}
